## Tensions
- **Accrual Method & Rate** – California requires an hourly accrual rate of 1 hr per 30 hrs worked, whereas New York mandates a fixed monthly accrual (8 hrs/month for ≥20 hrs/week employees and 2 hrs/month for <20 hrs/week). A single accrual schedule must satisfy both minimums without exceeding either.
- **Eligibility Thresholds** – California grants eligibility to all employees from day one, but New York ties eligibility to an employee’s average weekly hours in the preceding calendar year. Employees who are newly hired or part‑time may be eligible under CA yet not yet meet NY’s threshold, creating a compliance gray zone.
- **Maximum Accrual Limits** – California caps accrual at 48 hrs (or 24 days for <25 employees), while New York allows up to 40 days (320 hrs). The policy must cap leave at the lower statutory limit (48 hrs) so as not to give away more than CA permits, yet still respect NY’s higher ceiling.
- **Use Restrictions** – California’s language is broad (“any reason related to the health of the employee or a family member”), whereas New York enumerates specific categories but allows broader interpretation through case law. The wording must be inclusive enough for CA while not exceeding NY’s statutory scope.
- **PTO Substitution Prohibition** – California explicitly forbids using paid time off (PTO) as a substitute for sick leave; New York’s prohibition is inferred from case law. The policy must clearly separate the two benefits to avoid inadvertent substitution.

---

## Synthesis

Below is a single, unified written sick‑leave policy that satisfies both California and New York statutes while ensuring the company does not provide more leave than required in either jurisdiction. All numeric figures are **modeled at** their statutory minimums or caps; they are not guarantees of future law changes.

---

### 1. Purpose
This policy establishes the company’s compliance with the **Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act (HWHFA)** of California and the **Paid Sick Leave Law (PSLL)** of New York while maintaining a separate 10‑day paid time‑off (PTO) benefit.

### 2. Effective Date
[Insert date]

---

## 3. Eligibility

| Jurisdiction | Eligibility Criteria |
|--------------|----------------------|
| **California** | All employees, regardless of hours worked or employment status, are eligible to accrue sick leave from the first day of employment. |
| **New York – ≥20 hrs/week** | Employees whose average weekly hours in the preceding calendar year were **≥20 hrs** are eligible for accrual at the rates set below. |
| **New York – <20 hrs/week** | Employees whose average weekly hours in the preceding calendar year were **>0 but <20 hrs** are eligible for accrual at the lower rate below. |
| **New York – 0 hrs** | Employees who did not work any hours during the prior calendar year are **not** eligible to accrue sick leave under this policy. |

*The company will evaluate eligibility each pay period and adjust accruals accordingly.*

---

## 4. Accrual Rates

### 4.1 California
- **Rate:** **1 hour per 30 hrs worked** (modeled at the statutory minimum).  
- **Method:** Proportional to hours worked in each pay period; e.g., an employee who works 120 hrs in a month accrues 4 hrs of sick leave.

### 4.2 New York
| Average Weekly Hours | Monthly Accrual |
|-----------------------|-----------------|
| **≥20 hrs** | **8 hours (1 day)** per calendar month (modeled at the statutory minimum). |
| **<20 hrs** | **2 hours** per calendar month (modeled at the statutory minimum). |

*The company will not accrue sick leave at a rate higher than required by either statute; all accruals are limited to these minimum rates.*

---

## 5. Maximum Accrual Limits

| Jurisdiction | Cap |
|--------------|-----|
| **California** | **48 hrs** (or 24 days for employers with <25 employees). Unused leave may be carried over indefinitely up to this limit. |
| **New York** | **40 days (320 hrs)**. Any balance exceeding this cap at the end of a calendar year is forfeited. |

*The policy explicitly limits accruals to the lower statutory cap (48 hrs) so as not to exceed California’s maximum while remaining within New York’s higher ceiling.*

---

## 6. Use of Sick Leave

Sick leave may be used for:

- The employee’s own illness or injury, including preventive care and medical appointments.
- Illness or injury of a spouse, domestic partner, child, parent, grandparent, sibling, or other family member as defined by the statutes.
- Domestic violence or sexual assault situations (New York).

Employees must provide reasonable notice to their supervisor when possible; in emergencies, leave may be used without prior notice. **Sick leave is separate from the company’s 10‑day PTO benefit and cannot be substituted for it under California law**; New York case law also treats PTO as distinct.

---

## 7. Carryover & Forfeiture

- **California:** Unused sick leave may be carried over to subsequent years up to the statutory cap of 48 hrs; no forfeiture occurs unless an employee leaves before reaching the cap.
- **New York:** Employees may carry over unused sick leave up to the 40‑day limit; any balance above this threshold at year‑end is forfeited.

---

## 8. Recordkeeping & Notice

- The company will maintain accurate records of accrued, used, and remaining sick‑leave balances for each employee.
- **California:** Written notice of the policy must be provided within 30 days of employment; periodic updates are required as statutes change.
- **New York:** Employees receive an annual statement of their accrued balance or may request a written statement at any time by contacting Human Resources.

---

## 9. Enforcement & Disciplinary Action

Any retaliation against an employee for exercising rights under this policy is prohibited. Violations, including unauthorized use or failure to accrue leave as required, may result in disciplinary action up to and including termination.

---

### Caveat
The statutory provisions cited are accurate **as of the last update in 2023**. Employers should verify whether any amendments have been enacted since that date—particularly regarding accrual caps or eligibility thresholds—to ensure ongoing compliance.

**Key Differences Between the Two Statutes**

1. **Statutory Framework and Minimum Accrual Rate**  
   - *California – Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act (HWHFA)*: The statute requires employers to provide paid sick leave at a rate of **one hour for every 30 hours worked**. This accrual is calculated on an hourly basis and applies to all employees regardless of the number of hours worked in a pay period.  
   - *New York – Paid Sick Leave Law (PSLL)*: New York’s law also sets a minimum accrual rate of **one hour per 30 hours worked**, but it codifies this through a monthly accrual schedule that is contingent on an employee’s average weekly hours in the preceding calendar year. Employees who work **20 or more hours per week** accrue at least **one day (8 hours) per month**; those who work **less than 20 hours per week** accrue at least **two hours per month**.

2. **Eligibility Thresholds**  
   - California: All employees, including part‑time workers and seasonal hires, are eligible as soon as they begin employment.  
   - New York: Eligibility is tied to the employee’s average weekly hours in the preceding calendar year; employees who worked fewer than 20 hours per week for that entire year are not entitled to accrue sick leave under the PSLL.

3. **Maximum Accrual Limits**  
   - California caps accrual at **48 hours or 24 days (whichever is less)** for all employers, with a lower cap of 24 days for employers with fewer than 25 employees. Unused leave may be carried over indefinitely up to the cap.  
   - New York limits accrual to **40 days (320 hours)**. Employees may carry over unused sick leave up to this maximum; any balance above the cap is forfeited.

4. **Use Restrictions and Protected Reasons**  
   Both statutes allow use for an employee’s own illness or injury, a family member’s illness or injury, preventive care, and other specified circumstances (e.g., domestic violence in New York). California additionally requires that sick leave be available for “any reason related to the health of the employee or a family member,” whereas New York lists specific categories but allows broader interpretation through case law.

5. **Notice and Record‑Keeping Requirements**  
   - California mandates written notice of the policy within 30 days of employment, periodic updates, and record‑keeping of accruals and usage.  
   - New York requires a written statement of the employee’s accrued balance at least once per year or upon request, and employers must keep accurate records.

6. **Interaction with Other Leave**  
   California prohibits requiring employees to use paid time off (PTO) as a substitute for sick leave; the law treats PTO and sick leave as distinct entitlements. New York does not contain an explicit prohibition but case law has interpreted that PTO cannot be used in lieu of statutory sick leave.

- **California Employees:** All employees, regardless of hours worked or employment status, are eligible to accrue sick leave from the first day of employment.

  - *≥20 hours/week:* Eligible for accrual at the rate set below.  
  - *<20 hours/week but >0:* Eligible for accrual at the lower rate set below.  
  Employees who did not work any hours during the prior calendar year are not eligible to accrue sick leave under this policy.

---

#### 2. Accrual Rates

| Jurisdiction | Minimum Accrual Rate | Calculation Basis |
|--------------|----------------------|-------------------|
| **California** | **1 hour per 30 hours worked** | Proportional to hours worked in each pay period; e.g., an employee who works 120 hours in a month accrues 4 hours of sick leave. |
| **New York – ≥20 hrs/week** | **8 hours (1 day) per calendar month** | Fixed monthly accrual regardless of exact hours worked, provided the eligibility threshold is met. |
| **New York – <20 hrs/week** | **2 hours per calendar month** | Fixed monthly accrual for part‑time employees who meet the eligibility threshold. |

*The company will not accrue sick leave at a rate higher than required by either statute; all accruals are limited to the minimum rates above.*

---

#### 3. Maximum Accrual Limits

- **California:** Employees may accrue up to **48 hours** or **24 days**, whichever is less, for employers with 25 or more employees; for smaller employers the cap is **24 days**. Unused leave may be carried over indefinitely up to this limit.  
- **New York:** Employees may accrue up to **40 days (320 hours)**. Any balance exceeding this cap at the end of a calendar year is forfeited.

The policy explicitly limits accruals to these statutory caps; no employee will receive more leave than permitted by law.

---

- Sick leave may be used for:  
  - The employee’s own illness or injury, including preventive care and medical appointments.  
  - Illness or injury of a spouse, domestic partner, child, parent, grandparent, sibling, or other family member as defined by the statutes.  
  - Domestic violence or sexual assault situations (New York).  
- Employees must provide reasonable notice to their supervisor when possible; in emergencies, employees may use leave without prior notice.  
- Sick leave is **separate** from the company’s 10‑day PTO benefit and cannot be substituted for it under California law.

---

#### 5. Carryover and Forfeiture

- **California:** Unused sick leave may be carried over to subsequent years up to the statutory cap; no forfeiture occurs unless an employee leaves the company before reaching the cap.  
- **New York:** Employees may carry over unused sick leave up to the 40‑day limit; any balance above this threshold at year‑end is forfeited.

---

#### 6. Recordkeeping and Notice

- The company will maintain accurate records of accrued, used, and remaining sick leave balances for each employee.  
- California law requires written notice of the policy within 30 days of employment; New York law requires an annual statement of balance or upon request. Employees may obtain a written statement of their current sick‑leave balance at any time by contacting Human Resources.

---

#### 7. Enforcement and Disciplinary Action

- Any retaliation against an employee for exercising rights under this policy is prohibited.  
- Violations of the policy, including unauthorized use or failure to accrue leave as required, may result in disciplinary action up to and including termination.

A 60-person company with offices in California and New York wants one written sick-leave policy covering both sites. Both states' accrual statutes have been in force and unchanged for several years. 1. **Statutory Framework and Minimum Accrual Rate**  
   - *California – Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act (HWHFA)*: The statute requires employers to provide paid sick leave at a rate of **one hour for every 30 hours worked**. This accrual is calculated on an hourly basis and applies to all employees regardless of the number of hours worked in a pay period.  
   - *New York – Paid Sick Leave Law (PSLL)*: New York’s law also sets a minimum accrual rate of **one hour per 30 hours worked**, but it codifies this through a monthly accrual schedule that is contingent on an employee’s average weekly hours in the preceding calendar year. Employees who work **20 or more hours per week** accrue at least **one day (8 hours) per month**; those who work **less than 20 hours per week** accrue at least **two hours per month**.

2. **Eligibility Thresholds**  
   - California: All employees, including part‑time workers and seasonal hires, are eligible as soon as they begin employment.  
   - New York: Eligibility is tied to the employee’s average weekly hours in the preceding calendar year; employees who worked fewer than 20 hours per week for that entire year are not entitled to accrue sick leave under the PSLL.

   - California caps accrual at **48 hours or 24 days (whichever is less)** for all employers, with a lower cap of 24 days for employers with fewer than 25 employees. Unused leave may be carried over indefinitely up to the cap.

   - California mandates written notice of the policy within 30 days of employment, periodic updates, and record‑keeping of accruals and usage.  
   - New York requires a written statement of the employee’s accrued balance at least once per year or upon request, and employers must keep accurate records.

   California prohibits requiring employees to use paid time off (PTO) as a substitute for sick leave; the law treats PTO and sick leave as distinct entitlements. New York does not contain an explicit prohibition but case law has interpreted that PTO cannot be used in lieu of statutory sick leave.

**Effective Date:** [Insert date]

| Jurisdiction | Minimum Accrual Rate | Calculation Basis |
|--------------|----------------------|-------------------|
| **California** | **1 hour per 30 hours worked** | Proportional to hours worked in each pay period; e.g., an employee who works 120 hours in a month accrues 4 hours of sick leave. |
| **New York – ≥20 hrs/week** | **8 hours (1 day) per calendar month** | Fixed monthly accrual regardless of exact hours worked, provided the eligibility threshold is met. |
| **New York – <20 hrs/week** | **2 hours per calendar month** | Fixed monthly accrual for part‑time employees who meet the eligibility threshold. |

*The company will not accrue sick leave at a rate higher than required by either statute; all accruals are limited to the minimum rates above.*

---

#### 3. Maximum Accrual Limits

- **California:** Employees may accrue up to **48 hours** or **24 days**, whichever is less, for employers with 25 or more employees; for smaller employers the cap is **24 days**. Unused leave may be carried over indefinitely up to this limit.  
- **New York:** Employees may accrue up to **40 days (320 hours)**. Any balance exceeding this cap at the end of a calendar year is forfeited.

---

- Sick leave may be used for:  
  - The employee’s own illness or injury, including preventive care and medical appointments.  
  - Illness or injury of a spouse, domestic partner, child, parent, grandparent, sibling, or other family member as defined by the statutes.

---

- **California:** Unused sick leave may be carried over to subsequent years up to the statutory cap; no forfeiture occurs unless an employee leaves the company before reaching the cap.  
- **New York:** Employees may carry over unused sick leave up to the 40‑day limit; any balance above this threshold at year‑end is forfeited.

- Any retaliation against an employee for exercising rights under this policy is prohibited.

## Tensions
- **Accrual Method & Rate** – California requires an hourly accrual rate of 1 hr per 30 hrs worked, whereas New York mandates a fixed monthly accrual (8 hrs/month for ≥20 hrs/week employees and 2 hrs/month for <20 hrs/week). A single accrual schedule must satisfy both minimums without exceeding either.
- **Eligibility Thresholds** – California grants eligibility to all employees from day one, but New York ties eligibility to an employee’s average weekly hours in the preceding calendar year. Employees who are newly hired or part‑time may be eligible under CA yet not yet meet NY’s threshold, creating a compliance gray zone.
- **Maximum Accrual Limits** – California caps accrual at 48 hrs (or 24 days for <25 employees), while New York allows up to 40 days (320 hrs). The policy must cap leave at the lower statutory limit (48 hrs) so as not to give away more than CA permits, yet still respect NY’s higher ceiling.
- **Use Restrictions** – California’s language is broad (“any reason related to the health of the employee or a family member”), whereas New York enumerates specific categories but allows broader interpretation through case law. The wording must be inclusive enough for CA while not exceeding NY’s statutory scope.
- **PTO Substitution Prohibition** – California explicitly forbids using paid time off (PTO) as a substitute for sick leave; New York’s prohibition is inferred from case law. The policy must clearly separate the two benefits to avoid inadvertent substitution.

---

## Synthesis

Below is a single, unified written sick‑leave policy that satisfies both California and New York statutes while ensuring the company does not provide more leave than required in either jurisdiction. All numeric figures are **modeled at** their statutory minimums or caps; they are not guarantees of future law changes.

---

### 1. Purpose
This policy establishes the company’s compliance with the **Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act (HWHFA)** of California and the **Paid Sick Leave Law (PSLL)** of New York while maintaining a separate 10‑day paid time‑off (PTO) benefit.

### 2. Effective Date
[Insert date]

---

## 3. Eligibility

| Jurisdiction | Eligibility Criteria |
|--------------|----------------------|
| **California** | All employees, regardless of hours worked or employment status, are eligible to accrue sick leave from the first day of employment. |
| **New York – ≥20 hrs/week** | Employees whose average weekly hours in the preceding calendar year were **≥20 hrs** are eligible for accrual at the rates set below. |
| **New York – <20 hrs/week** | Employees whose average weekly hours in the preceding calendar year were **>0 but <20 hrs** are eligible for accrual at the lower rate below. |
| **New York – 0 hrs** | Employees who did not work any hours during the prior calendar year are **not** eligible to accrue sick leave under this policy. |

*The company will evaluate eligibility each pay period and adjust accruals accordingly.*

---

## 4. Accrual Rates

### 4.1 California
- **Rate:** **1 hour per 30 hrs worked** (modeled at the statutory minimum).  
- **Method:** Proportional to hours worked in each pay period; e.g., an employee who works 120 hrs in a month accrues 4 hrs of sick leave.

### 4.2 New York
| Average Weekly Hours | Monthly Accrual |
|-----------------------|-----------------|
| **≥20 hrs** | **8 hours (1 day)** per calendar month (modeled at the statutory minimum). |
| **<20 hrs** | **2 hours** per calendar month (modeled at the statutory minimum). |

*The company will not accrue sick leave at a rate higher than required by either statute; all accruals are limited to these minimum rates.*

---

## 5. Maximum Accrual Limits

| Jurisdiction | Cap |
|--------------|-----|
| **California** | **48 hrs** (or 24 days for employers with <25 employees). Unused leave may be carried over indefinitely up to this limit. |
| **New York** | **40 days (320 hrs)**. Any balance exceeding this cap at the end of a calendar year is forfeited. |

*The policy explicitly limits accruals to the lower statutory cap (48 hrs) so as not to exceed California’s maximum while remaining within New York’s higher ceiling.*

---

## 6. Use of Sick Leave

Sick leave may be used for:

- The employee’s own illness or injury, including preventive care and medical appointments.
- Illness or injury of a spouse, domestic partner, child, parent, grandparent, sibling, or other family member as defined by the statutes.
- Domestic violence or sexual assault situations (New York).

Employees must provide reasonable notice to their supervisor when possible; in emergencies, leave may be used without prior notice. **Sick leave is separate from the company’s 10‑day PTO benefit and cannot be substituted for it under California law**; New York case law also treats PTO as distinct.

---

## 7. Carryover & Forfeiture

- **California:** Unused sick leave may be carried over to subsequent years up to the statutory cap of 48 hrs; no forfeiture occurs unless an employee leaves before reaching the cap.
- **New York:** Employees may carry over unused sick leave up to the 40‑day limit; any balance above this threshold at year‑end is forfeited.

---

## 8. Recordkeeping & Notice

- The company will maintain accurate records of accrued, used, and remaining sick‑leave balances for each employee.
- **California:** Written notice of the policy must be provided within 30 days of employment; periodic updates are required as statutes change.
- **New York:** Employees receive an annual statement of their accrued balance or may request a written statement at any time by contacting Human Resources.

---

## 9. Enforcement & Disciplinary Action

Any retaliation against an employee for exercising rights under this policy is prohibited. Violations, including unauthorized use or failure to accrue leave as required, may result in disciplinary action up to and including termination.

---

### Caveat
The statutory provisions cited are accurate **as of the last update in 2023**. Employers should verify whether any amendments have been enacted since that date—particularly regarding accrual caps or eligibility thresholds—to ensure ongoing compliance.
